newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia officials welcome foreign aid pledge.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia officials welcome foreign aid pledge.

text.p: Cambodian officials on Thursday welcomed a pledge of $450 million in official foreign aid, made despite donors' concerns about political instability in the country.
"I think the international community remains committed and interested in Cambodia," said Nady Tan, secretary general of the Council of Ministers.
"They have entrusted us with the process of rehabilitating and reconstructing the country," he told Reuters.
Donors announced the 1997/98 package at the end of a two-day meeting held under the auspices of the World Bank in Paris on Wednesday.
Cambodia received official aid pledges of $500 million for 1996/97.
The donors called on Cambodia to tackle issues which they said had seen little progress over the past year but they stopped short of tying aid to specific reforms.

World Bank official Javad Shirazi told reporters in Paris that Cambodia needed to adopt more effective tax collection and accounting methods to ensure the fiscal system was clear and fair, and gather more revenue from logging activities.

"Cambodia is entering a critical phase in the run-up to elections," he said. "The government needs to focus on economic reforms" and ensure "political issues do not destabilise the gains that have been made", he added.
A power struggle between the two leaders of the deadlocked coalition government has led to increasing concern about political stability and violence.

The United Nations warned in a statement from its representatives in Cambodia, released in Phnom Penh on Wednesday, that the government was spending too much money on security forces and failing to meet tax revenue collection targets.
There had been suggestions from some donor countries that aid be linked to an improved political climate.
But analysts said political and administrative problems were unlikely to derail Cambodia's foreign aid programme, which accounts for half of the national budget.
"There was tough talk, but it was not translated into significant penalties," said one diplomat in Phnom Penh.

"They (the donors) aren't being listened to much, but they can't withdraw at this stage of the game... They'll stick with Cambodia through the elections so they don't seem responsible for the situation if it gets worse," he added.
